text: I’ll treat the stated 8 mm cell width as the clear opening across flats; adding the 1 mm wall gives a 9 mm centre pitch across flats. Flow will be along +x, with the core at x=0–20 mm, inlet at x=-40 mm, and outlet at x=100 mm. I’ll first lay out the clipped hexagonal array and inspect the coarse geometry before meshing.

The array uses a pointy-sided hexagon in the y–z cross-section, with 9 mm pitch between opposite cell rows. I’m now constructing the 20 mm core as a square slab minus all clear hexagonal prisms that intersect its section, and plotting the opening layout against the 80 mm duct boundary.

The layout picture is correct, but the solid-volume check exposed that subtracting a generic compound did not execute the intended Boolean—the reported volume was still the full slab volume. I’m correcting that by using the kernel’s multi-tool cut operation and will verify both open area and wall thickness numerically before export.
I’ll re-emit the rejected construction in a replay-safe form and test a single opening cut first; this isolates whether the issue is the prism construction or the aggregate Boolean.

The aggregate Boolean was not the problem: the test prism had zero volume because the 3D polygon was not being promoted to a planar sketch as intended. I’ll construct the hexagon explicitly on `Plane.YZ` and verify one prism’s analytical volume before rebuilding the array.
`Polygon` already creates a planar face in this build123d version, so wrapping it in `Face(...)` emptied the shape. I’ll use it directly and repeat the analytical volume check.
With a valid prism established, I’ll rebuild all 105 openings and perform the cut. The resulting wall solid should occupy only a modest fraction of the 20 × 80 × 80 mm slab, not 100%.

The corrected core has a 20.5% solid fraction and remains one connected wall solid. I’ll render it together with a translucent outline of the full duct so the flow direction, core placement, and edge clipping can be checked visually before meshing.

The preview confirms the wall network spans the full 20 mm core thickness and is clipped by the 80 mm square duct. I’ll now export that wall solid as STEP in metres, subtract it from the complete 140 mm-long duct volume in Gmsh, and inspect the resulting boundary-surface classification before generating tetrahedra.

Gmsh’s OCC bounding boxes are padded by about \(10^{-7}\) m, so the initial \(10^{-8}\) m classification tolerance was intentionally too strict and assigned everything to the fallback group. I’ll repeat with a \(10^{-6}\) m tolerance, create the four named physical surface groups, and generate a coarse tetrahedral mesh (4 mm target away from geometry-imposed smaller edges).

The coarse mesh has 29,674 nodes and about 144k tetrahedra; all 556 boundary surfaces were assigned exactly once to the requested patches. I’ll convert it to OpenFOAM, normalize the physical-group patch types to `patch`, and run the binding `checkMesh` quality/topology check.

Conversion succeeded with the four named Gmsh groups. The “undefined faces” message is Gmsh-to-OpenFOAM’s normal pre-matching stage, but I’ll inspect the final boundary counts to ensure `defaultFaces` is empty. `checkMesh -allGeometry` also requires placeholder discretization dictionaries in this OpenFOAM release, so I’ll add minimal valid ones and rerun it.

Topology, patch coverage, dimensions, and volume are correct, but the exhaustive geometry check flags tetrahedral determinant/interpolation metrics (despite Gmsh reporting no ill-shaped tetrahedra). I’ll confirm the binding plain `checkMesh` result before deciding whether a different 3D algorithm or optimization pass is needed.

Plain `checkMesh` passes (“Mesh OK”); only the optional exhaustive tetra determinant metrics warn. I’ll now export each already-named OpenFOAM boundary patch to its own STL, ensuring the delivered surface files correspond exactly to the mesh patches rather than being reclassified afterward.

`foamToSurface` in this release exports all patches together and offers no selection option. I’ll use `surfaceMeshExtract`, which preserves patch zones, inspect its syntax, then split/export the four zones if needed.
`surfaceMeshExtract` supports exact patch selection. I’ll export the four patches to `constant/triSurface`, then verify that their triangle totals equal the OpenFOAM boundary-face total.

The four STL files contain 28,544 triangles in total, exactly matching the mesh boundary count. I’ll make one final colored boundary rendering from those delivered files and report the measured mesh bounds and patch areas as a last geometry check.

The delivered mesh is a single connected air region with 140,362 tetrahedra and four nonempty named patches. Plain `checkMesh` reports **Mesh OK**; the optional `-allTopology -allGeometry` run additionally flagged 3,877 low-determinant tetrahedra and 4 low-interpolation-weight faces, which I am reporting rather than hiding. Geometry bounds, patch coverage, cell dimensions, and core thickness were all measured.
